tagline: Mountain schools and cross-shaped stones mark this corner of Virginia.
intro: The Blue Ridge foothills hold Ferrum College, while Fairy Stone State Park lies in Patrick County. The park takes its name from the cross-shaped staurolite stones found in its vicinity.
In Ferrum, a school established in 1913 served mountain communities with primary and secondary education. The railway built a cinder road from the depot to the school as the institution grew.

Callaway has a Greek Revival church with paired front entrances; Ferrum has a college museum devoted to Blue Ridge folklore. Fairy Stone State Park adds a lake and structures built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, with many of those structures still in use.

moments.title: Callaway
moments.text: Two front entrances, shuttered windows and a pedimented gable distinguish Piedmont Presbyterian Church in Callaway. Benjamin Deyerle built the Greek Revival church about 1850. Outside Callaway, Phoebe Needles Mission School served children who could not reach public schools in Callaway, Ferrum or Rocky Mount. Its later uses continue that educational connection: the former school is now a church parish, a Center for Lifelong Learning and a summer camp operated by the Episcopal Diocese of Southwestern Virginia. The mission school’s location answered a transport problem: the state school system had no public transport for these children.

moments.title: Ferrum
moments.text: Ferrum College began as a mountain school, with its first classes held in John Wesley Hall in the fall of 1914. The railway built a cinder road connecting the depot and school. The institution moved from primary and secondary teaching into higher education, receiving accreditation as a four-year college in 1976. Regional culture also has a place on campus: the Blue Ridge Institute and Museum became the State Center for Blue Ridge Folklore in 1986. The institute has held its annual Blue Ridge Folklife Festival since 1973 to showcase regional traditions.

moments.title: Fairy Stone State Park
moments.text: Cross-shaped staurolite gives Fairy Stone State Park its name. Junius B. Fishburn, a former owner of the Roanoke Times, donated the land in 1933. Three years later, it opened with Virginia’s first six state parks on June 15, 1936. The Civilian Conservation Corps built the lake and many structures that remain in use. At 4,741 acres, it was the largest of those six original parks.
